meta.subtitle: Second-quarter 2026 earnings rose on lower catastrophes, investment income and Personal Lines; commercial current-year ratios rose in the quarter

analystSentiment.commentary:
The Hanover's second quarter of 2026 was a solid quarter with one soft spot. Net income was $191.6 million against $157.1 million a year earlier, and over the half year the underlying book improved, not just the weather (see Financials).

The soft spot is commercial. Core Commercial and Specialty current-year ratios rose in the second quarter against prior-year quarters the company says benefited from lighter property losses, and the company increased loss ratio selections in Core Commercial liability coverages. That matters because Core Commercial is where premium growth is accelerating.

The stock trades at 10.5x trailing earnings and below the $238.25 consensus target, while consensus expects earnings to step down from here, and the CEO plans to retire at the end of 2026. The rating is HOLD, with the probability-weighted value close to the current price; the scenario argument sits in the valuation section.

executiveSummary.companyOverview:
The Hanover Insurance Group, Inc. is a property and casualty insurer founded in 1852 and headquartered in Worcester, Massachusetts. It sells to individuals and businesses in the United States through independent agents and brokers. The company was formerly known as Allmerica Financial Corp. and took its current name in December 2005. Its principal property and casualty companies are Hanover Insurance and Citizens Insurance Company of America.

The company reports four segments: Core Commercial, Specialty, Personal Lines and Other. The vendor data carries it as one consolidated line, with FY25 revenue of $6.6B and FY25 net income of $662.5M. The proxy reports FY25 net written premium of $6,322.1 million; that is a premium measure on a different basis from vendor revenue, and the two should not be read as one series.

The view: this is a diversified commercial and personal lines carrier whose earnings swing with weather, loss-cost trends and reserve development more than with premium volume, which is the lens for everything that follows.

thesis.label: HOLD
thesis.body:
HOLD, target range $210 to $245.

- Returns are high, and the underlying book improved over the six months ended June 30, 2026 (see Financials).
- Core Commercial and Specialty current-year ratios rose in the second quarter; whether that is a comparison effect or the start of a trend is the open question.
- Consensus expects forward earnings below trailing earnings, which limits re-rating at 10.5x trailing (see Valuation).
- The probability-weighted value sits close to the current price; the weighting is in Valuation.

catalysts: Continued share repurchases under the authorization announced May 13, 2026; covered under Management.
Personal Lines pricing that keeps earning through into loss ratios; see Growth.
Higher earned yields lifting investment income; see Growth.
A planned CEO handover at the end of 2026; see Management.
risks: Catastrophes: 2026 catastrophe losses have run below 2025 so far, and a heavier storm season would reverse that.
Commercial loss picks: Core Commercial and Specialty current-year ratios rose in the second quarter of 2026.
Reserve releases: favorable prior-year development grew in 2026 and could shrink.
Bond marks: net unrealized losses on fixed maturities widened in the quarter, weighing on book value; see the balance sheet discussion.

income.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.incomeCommentary:
The five-year vendor table shows how volatile this earnings stream is. Diluted EPS went from $11.60 in FY21 to $3.21 in FY22 and $0.98 in FY23, then recovered to $11.70 in FY24 and $18.16 in FY25. Operating margin followed the same path, bottoming in FY23 and reaching 14.1% in FY25. Neither source explains the FY22 to FY23 trough. Revenue rose in every year shown, so the swings are a margin story.

The second quarter of 2026 extended the recovery. Net income per diluted share was $5.38 against $4.30, and operating income per diluted share was $5.31 against $4.35. The combined ratio was 91.2% against 92.5%, with the catastrophe ratio at 5.7% against 7.0%, while the prior-year development ratio was (1.3)% against (1.2)%, close to flat. The company attributes the quarter's operating income gain to lower catastrophe losses, higher net investment income (see Growth) and current accident year improvement driven by Personal Lines. Over the six months, the current accident year combined ratio excluding catastrophes improved to 86.9% from 87.9%, the catastrophe ratio was 6.0% against 6.7%, and favorable development was slightly larger. Current-year underwriting is a real part of the half-year gain.

By segment, Personal Lines' current accident year loss and LAE ratio excluding catastrophes decreased 4.2 points, to 55.6%, which the company attributes to earned pricing outpacing loss trends, benign property claims frequency and lower homeowners large losses. Core Commercial's equivalent loss ratio was 58.7%, 2.2 points above the prior-year quarter but 0.4 points better than full-year 2025; the company increased loss ratio selections in liability coverages and says the prior-year quarter benefited from lower-than-usual property losses. For the six months, Core Commercial's current accident year combined ratio excluding catastrophes improved to 91.3% from 92.3%. Specialty's equivalent ratio of 51.6% rose 2.6 points, which the company calls consistent with its long-term expectations. The commercial rise is a one-quarter move against an easy comparison; the liability loss-pick increase is the part that bears watching.

Net income and operating income per share were close for the six months, at $10.58 and $10.55, so GAAP and operating earnings are not diverging materially this year.

balance.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.balanceCommentary:
For an insurer, book value and the investment portfolio matter more than the vendor's debt lines. Book value per share was $105.40 at June 30, 2026, up 3.5% from March 31, 2026. Excluding net unrealized depreciation on fixed maturity investments, net of tax, it was $111.26. The gap is the bond-mark overhang: net unrealized losses on the fixed maturity portfolio were $259.5 million before income taxes at June 30, 2026, against $235.6 million at March 31, 2026. The release says the higher unrealized loss partly offset the quarter's earnings in book value, so bond marks are a live drag on the reported equity base.

The portfolio is conservative on the company's own description: $11.2 billion of cash and invested assets at June 30, 2026, with fixed maturities and cash approximately 93% of the portfolio and approximately 95% of fixed maturities rated investment grade. Statutory capital and surplus of the operating insurance company was $3.54 billion at the same date, slightly higher than at March 31, 2026.

On the vendor's annual figures, total equity dipped to $2.3B in FY22 and reached $3.6B in FY25; the table does not give the cause of the dip. The vendor shows total debt higher in FY25 than in FY24, offset by $1.1B of cash and short-term investments, for net debt of $0.1B. Neither the vendor table nor the excerpts say why debt rose. Interest expense on debt was $10.1 million in the second quarter of 2026 against $8.6 million a year earlier, a small line next to operating income, so leverage is not the constraint on these figures; catastrophe and reserve risk are.

cashflow.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.cashflowCommentary:
Operating cash flow rose to $1.2B in FY25 from $0.8B in FY24, and with negligible capital expenditure the vendor's free cash flow matches it, a 17.7% FCF margin. The series is uneven: FCF margin fell to 5.8% in FY23 before recovering, alongside the earnings trough in the income table.

For an insurer, operating cash flow is not the same as earnings available for distribution, so the TTM FCF yield of 16.4% should not be read as payout capacity. Dividends and repurchases are the better gauge of what reaches shareholders, and they are covered under Management.

These are vendor-derived measures, and the excerpts do not describe any statutory limits on dividends from the insurance subsidiaries to the holding company, so how much of this cash can reach the holding company cannot be judged from the data.

multiples.note: Peer multiples pending a peer data source.

valuation.multiplesCommentary:
THG trades at 10.5x trailing earnings, 10.8x NTM earnings and ~11.2x FY27E, with P/S of 1.1x and EV/EBITDA of 8.0x. The forward multiples sit above the trailing one because consensus forward earnings are below trailing earnings. The FY27E multiple is higher again because consensus EPS steps down from $20.39 for FY26E to $19.61 for FY27E. The estimates do not say why, and their basis, GAAP or operating, is not stated. The Street, in other words, expects earnings to come down from the current level, which caps how far the multiple can expand.

Book value is the more relevant yardstick for an insurer. The stock trades well above book value per share of $105.40 at June 30, 2026. That premium rests on returns: the company reported net return on equity of 21.0% for the six months ended June 30, 2026, and the proxy reports FY25 net return on equity of 20.6%, so returns have held at about the FY25 level. A premium to book holds only while they stay there, and the FY23 trough in the income table shows they need not.

The dividend yield is 1.75%. No peer multiples are available in the data, so no relative-valuation claim is made. On these multiples the stock is not expensive for returns at the current level.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: Anchored to the Street high target of $260.00 on a one-year horizon. The half-year current-year improvement carries into commercial lines, the second-quarter commercial rise proves a comparison effect, catastrophes stay moderate and repurchases keep shrinking the share count, so FY27E consensus EPS proves conservative and the stock re-rates toward the top of the Street range.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Anchored to the Street low target of $229.00 on a one-year horizon. FY26E consensus EPS is delivered and commercial loss picks hold at current levels, so the stock moves modestly toward the bottom of the Street range; the consensus EPS step-down into FY27E keeps it short of the consensus target.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: Near the 52-week low of $166.54 on a one-year horizon. A heavier catastrophe year, further commercial loss-pick increases and fading favorable development push EPS to somewhere between FY24's $11.70 and FY25's $18.16, and the stock holds its 10.5x trailing multiple on that lower base.

valuation.scenarioCommentary:
The stock is at $219.43. Base carries 50%, Bull 30% and Bear 20%. The three scenarios are alternative outcomes for the next year, not additive. Bull gets the larger tail weight because the half-year current-year improvement in the income discussion is real. Bear keeps a meaningful weight for three reasons the data does support: Core Commercial and Specialty current-year ratios rose in the second quarter with a liability loss-pick increase; favorable reserve development is a source of earnings that can stop; and the FY22 to FY23 EPS series shows how quickly a bad year can arrive for this company.

The Bear sits further below Base than the Bull sits above it. The probability-weighted fair value therefore lands below Base and only modestly above the current price, while the Bear implies a fall back toward the 52-week low. Expected upside is too thin relative to that downside to support a BUY, and nothing in the quarter argues for a SELL. The rating is HOLD, with a target range of $210 to $245 that brackets Base.

The consensus target of $238.25 sits above Base. Base, as its driver says, gives weight to the consensus EPS step-down into FY27E that the Street's own targets appear to look through.

What would move the call: an upgrade needs Core Commercial's current accident year loss and LAE ratio excluding catastrophes to hold at or below its second-quarter 2026 level through the second half of 2026, with no further liability loss-pick increases. A downgrade follows if liability loss picks rise again and favorable development shrinks at the same time.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: The vendor carries THG as one consolidated line, with FY25 revenue of $6.6B. The company reports four segments, Core Commercial, Specialty, Personal Lines and Other, and no revenue split between them is quoted here. Core Commercial serves small businesses and the middle market with account-based coverage. Specialty spans four divisions (Marine and Industrial Property, Professional and Executive Lines, E&S and Alternative Markets, and Surety and Other) sold mainly through independent agents, including wholesalers. Personal Lines sells auto, homeowners and other personal coverages through agencies focused on total account solutions. Other holds holding-company items and run-off businesses. The mix spreads exposure across commercial and personal risks, but every segment shares the same independent-agent channel and the same US weather.

moatFactors.name: Independent-agent relationships
moatFactors.body: The company's stated strategy centers on select independent agents, with expansion of the agency footprint in underpenetrated geographies as warranted. That relationship model is the core of the franchise. The excerpts give no agent count, retention or share-of-wallet data, so whether it confers pricing power cannot be tested from the data.

moatFactors.name: Account-based personal lines
moatFactors.body: Approximately 89% of Personal Lines policies in force are with customers holding multiple policies or coverages with the company, which is the basis of this factor. No retention data is provided to show whether multi-policy accounts renew at higher rates, and policies in force were flat sequentially in the second quarter of 2026 (see Growth), so durability cannot be confirmed from the data.

moatFactors.name: Specialty breadth
moatFactors.body: Specialty gives agents placement options that complement Core Commercial accounts, which the company says enhances agent value. Specialty renewal price increases trailed the other two operating segments in the second quarter of 2026, so the breadth is not translating into pricing leverage this year.

businessMoat.durability: Returns through the cycle are the test of any insurer's moat. The FY23 earnings trough (see Financials) shows how quickly a year's earnings can disappear, and the premium to book rests on returns staying near current levels (see Valuation). Geographic concentration, covered under Risks, adds to the volatility. The rating is NARROW: agency relationships and the account focus support solid returns in normal years, but they offer no protection against weather or loss-cost inflation, which is what drives the bad years.

points: Premium growth picked up in the second quarter of 2026: {+ consolidated net premiums written grew 4.6% +}, against 3.9% for the six months. Core Commercial led, {+ up 7.2% +}, which the company calls an acceleration from the prior quarter, with middle market growth of 9.4% (approximately 7% excluding non-recurring items). The tension is that Core Commercial's current accident year loss and LAE ratio excluding catastrophes rose in the same quarter (see Financials), so the test is whether this growth is written at adequate margins.

Personal Lines net premiums written rose 2.6% in the second quarter of 2026, which the company attributes primarily to higher new business and, to a lesser extent, renewal price increases. Renewal price increases were 8.7% in Personal Lines, 7.8% in Core Commercial and 3.6% in Specialty; the release credits earned pricing for the Personal Lines current-year improvement described in Financials. Policies in force were essentially flat against the prior quarter, a sequential comparison to watch.

Investment income is the steadier lever. {+ Net investment income of $119.6 million rose 13.4% +} in the second quarter of 2026, which the company attributes to investing operating cash flows and higher earned yields; the total pre-tax earned yield was 4.28% against 4.11%. This grows independently of underwriting, but the 2025 10-K lists interest-rate fluctuations among the factors that affect investment returns, so lower rates would slow it.

Consensus expects revenue of $6.7B for FY26E and $7.1B for FY27E, while EPS steps down over the same period (see Valuation). The Street is therefore modeling top-line growth with narrower margins. The estimates do not say why margins would narrow, and this report does not attribute it.

management.leadership:
John C. Roche, president and chief executive officer, said in the July 28, 2026 earnings release that he plans to retire at the end of 2026, referring to an announcement made earlier in July 2026 that is not in the data. He said he and Dick Lavey will work closely together through the rest of the year for a seamless transition, and that Lavey's leadership, expertise and strategic vision position him well to successfully lead The Hanover into its next chapter. The excerpt does not state Lavey's future title. The 2026 proxy statement, dated March 26, 2026, lists Richard W. Lavey as EVP and Chief Operating Officer and Jeffrey M. Farber as EVP and Chief Financial Officer among the 2025 named executive officers.

The release language points toward continuity with an internal executive rather than a reset. Against that, any handover adds execution risk in a year when Core Commercial liability loss picks are rising, and the excerpts say nothing about the incoming team's priorities. Still to come: confirmation of the successor's title and any change in capital or underwriting targets.
management.capitalAllocation:
Capital return is accelerating. The company repurchased approximately 291,000 shares in the second quarter of 2026 for approximately $55 million, and approximately 827,000 shares for approximately $149 million year-to-date through July 24, 2026. That year-to-date total already exceeds the FY25 full-year repurchases. About $660 million remains under the new $700 million authorization announced May 13, 2026, and ending shares outstanding were 34.9 million against 35.9 million a year earlier.

For FY25, the proxy dated March 26, 2026 reports dividends of $130.6 million and repurchases of approximately 754,000 shares for $130.1 million; the vendor's cash flow table shows $129.2M of repurchases, and the proxy figure is used here. In 2025, per the same proxy, the quarterly dividend was raised 5.6% to $0.95 per share, or $3.80 annualized.

The CFO says profitability is building capital and enabling increased repurchases. Buying back stock above book value lowers book value per share mechanically, so these repurchases add value only if returns on equity stay near current levels. A catastrophe-heavy year would test whether the pace holds.
management.governance:
Governance detail comes from the 2026 proxy statement dated March 26, 2026. The board determined that every director and director nominee is independent except Mr. Roche, the president and CEO. The board reviewed Mr. Donnell's past role as President and CEO of NCCI, an organization the company does regular business with, and concluded he is independent; the proxy also notes that Richard W. Lavey served on the NCCI board until May 2025. Since 2021 the board has added four directors and four have retired. The excerpt does not say whether Mr. Roche will remain on the board after retiring.

Pay is weighted to returns. The 2025 short-term incentive funded at 140.0% of target. Return on equity PBRSUs for 2023 to 2025 paid at the 150.0% maximum on a three-year average Adjusted Operating ROE of 15.4%. Relative total shareholder return PBRSUs paid at 100.0% of target, with three-year total shareholder return of 42.57% at the 50th percentile of a pre-identified peer set. Say-on-pay support has exceeded 95% of shares cast in every year of the vote.

The structure is shareholder-friendly on independence. The watch item for outside holders is whether future ROE targets adjust for favorable reserve development, which grew in the six months ended June 30, 2026.
management.insiderOwnership: The proxy excerpt carries no beneficial ownership table and lists no 5% holders, and no Schedule 13G filings are in the data, so insider and outside-holder stakes cannot be stated. No controlling holder is identified. For outside shareholders, that means influence runs through annual votes rather than through any dominant owner, and there is no evidence either way on how much of management's wealth is tied to the stock.

idiosyncratic: Catastrophe load. Pre-tax catastrophe losses were $190.7 million for the six months ended June 30, 2026, against $203.1 million a year earlier, primarily from severe convective storms. That total included $61.7 million of favorable prior-year catastrophe development, against $18.0 million, largely related to 2025 events. Reported catastrophe losses were therefore lowered by releases on older events, which may not recur, and a heavier storm season would raise them. Watch the catastrophe ratio and any prior-year catastrophe development in the third quarter of 2026.

Commercial liability loss trends. The company increased loss ratio selections in Core Commercial liability coverages in the second quarter of 2026, and the 2025 10-K names social inflation and financed litigation among the developments that can raise claim payouts. The half-year comparison is still favorable (see Financials), but if liability picks keep rising, the segment where premium growth is accelerating adds premium at thinner margins. Watch Core Commercial's current accident year loss and LAE ratio excluding catastrophes and further loss-pick changes.

Reliance on reserve releases. Net favorable development on prior years' non-catastrophe reserves was $46.5 million for the six months ended June 30, 2026, against $38.2 million. The CFO says continued favorable development reinforces confidence in the reserve position; the filing excerpts give no independent measure of reserve adequacy, and none is inferred here. If releases shrink, earnings lose a support that has run through both periods. Watch the prior-year development ratio by segment.

Geographic concentration. The 2025 10-K, filed February 20, 2026, says a significant portion of net premiums written and earnings comes from Michigan, Massachusetts and other Northeast states, and a significant amount of Core Commercial and Specialty premium from California and Texas. It notes that California's Insurance Commissioner has taken steps to limit non-renewal of property policies in wildfire-prone areas. Regional weather or regulatory action in those states would hit the whole company. Watch rate filings and regulatory actions in those states.
risks.systemic: The 2025 10-K risk factors describe the industry-wide pressures. Costs that rise after policies are priced, including construction, automobile repair and medical costs, can come from inflation, supply-chain disruption or tariffs, and squeeze margins until pricing catches up. Competitive and regulatory pressures affect pricing and the risks covered. Interest-rate moves affect investment returns, and demand for property and casualty insurance varies with economic activity. The filing also notes that new catastrophe models assume more frequent and severe weather events and that rating agencies emphasize capital and reinsurance adequacy for geographically concentrated insurers, which could raise capital needs or limit growth. The practical read: the company's current pricing momentum is a response to these pressures, and the signal to watch is whether renewal price increases stay ahead of loss-cost trends.

body: HOLD; the scenario weighting, the comparison with the Street and the upgrade and downgrade triggers are set out in the valuation section.

Signals to watch over the next two quarters: Core Commercial's current accident year loss and LAE ratio excluding catastrophes, the size of favorable prior-year development, the catastrophe ratio through the storm season, and confirmation of the CEO successor's title.
